answers.1: Phones in Georgia public high schools. The main decision is already made: a state law, HB 1009, bans students from using phones or similar devices for the whole school day, including breaks and time between classes. The House and Senate passed it, and the governor signed it on May 5, 2026. It takes effect Dec 31, 2026, and high schools must start the ban by July 1, 2027 at the latest. What's still open is the details: each school district (or local school board) decides things like where phones are kept, and must adopt its policy by Jan 1, 2027. State lawmakers could also keep or change the law later. What confused me: the home page lists it under 'Decisions you can act on' even though it's already law. I can't tell when my own kid's school will start, or what 'takes effect Dec 31' means if schools have until July 1. And it doesn't say what happens to a student caught using a phone.
answers.2: The page doesn't say. For this law I saw nothing about fees, taxes, fines or anything families must buy, and nothing on whether storing phones costs families anything. It also doesn't say why. Each option on the Options tab has a 'who pays' part, but it's hidden until you tap, and I can't tell whether 'pays' means money or just giving something up (the tab talks about 'who gains or gives up what').
answers.3: None that the page mentions. It doesn't say any money goes to schools or comes from families. The Georgia Department of Education must give schools 'guidance and technical support', but no money is mentioned. (The other home page items, the PSC fuel-cost case and the Fulton County budget, do involve money, but they're separate from the phone law.)
answers.4: Three things. 1) Ask my school district or local school board how it will store phones, run off-campus activities, handle emergency contact and check whether the rules work. The home page says to do this before Jan 1, 2027, because districts must adopt their policies by Jan 1 each year. 2) Tell my state representative and senator whether to keep or change the law. No deadline is given. 3) Check my school's handbook or website for the rules. No date is given for when they'll be posted. But the page gives no phone number, email or meeting date for my district, and it can't tell me who my state lawmakers are ('Find my districts' isn't built yet), so I'd have to track down who to contact myself.
answers.5: The page doesn't explain them where I can see them; the meaning is behind a 'How to read these cards' link I'd have to tap. Going by the plain words: 'Supported' seems to mean evidence backs it up. 'Supported, with limits' seems to mean some evidence with a catch (the test-score study was in Florida, and there are no Georgia results yet). 'Uncertain' seems to mean there isn't enough evidence to say. 'Not mainly factual' seems to mean it's about values, not facts (that card says 'This is mainly a question of values'). Two cards say 'Evidence, by part' and show both Supported and Uncertain without saying which part gets which; I guessed the first sentence is the Supported part and the 'no data' sentence is the Uncertain part. I also wasn't sure whether the little tags after sentences (Law, Our analysis, Our framing) are evidence labels too; I think they show where each sentence came from.
answers.6: For: 'The ban will help students learn.' Supporters say fewer distractions mean more learning, and a Florida study found phone bans led to better test scores in the second year (no Georgia results yet). Against: 'Families lose direct contact with students during the school day.' Families would have to reach their kids through the school, and the page says there's no data on how that affects safety in a crisis.

seemed_to_favor: Mostly it felt even: three arguments for and three against, the same layout for each, and it admits weak evidence on both sides (no Georgia results yet; the England study found no well-being difference; no data on crisis safety or staff workload). If anything leaned, it leaned toward the law: the Arguments tab opens with 70.8% of parents supporting a ban and the lopsided votes (145 to 20, 52 to 0, no senator against the final bill) before any argument, so the law looks like the popular side before I read either case. The 'against' side also rests mostly on one named teacher, while four officials and a student spoke for the law, though the page says that reflects who its sources quoted, not how many people feel each way. I didn't see any political party mentioned.
hardest: Question 2 (cost). The page never mentions money for this law, and the only hint is a 'who pays' link I'd have to tap, so I can't tell whether the silence means it's free for families or just not covered; question 5 was close, because the label meanings are also behind a tap.
